what: The footer says every program was also built with clang++ 18.1 and gave identical results, but 34 of the chapter's 40 programs are .cmd projects whose 'secondary' run used the same g++ commands again. clang never built them.
evidence: Footer: "Every program was also built with clang++ 18.1 for comparison: all outputs that ran were identical, and only two compiler messages differ". capture.py run_program() L366-367: for a .cmd it only prepends the secondary tool's folder (/usr/bin) to PATH, and the .cmd steps hard-code `g++`. So the secondary run is g++ again: no `alt` is recorded for any .cmd program (clash, libfirst, exforgot, ...). Only arrivals, boss_trace, import_std, spot_macro, square_macro and trace_static (no .cmd) really ran on clang. The same thing is visible in ch29: prof.cpp's alt, labelled "clang++ 18.1", records `g++ -std=c++23 -O2 -pg prof.cpp -o prof`.
fix: Reword the footer: "The six single-file programs were also built with clang++ 18.1 (identical except import_std.cpp and spot_macro.cpp). The multi-file builds use g++ and GNU ld only." Engine fix: in capture.py, for cpp .cmd programs on the secondary, either substitute g++→clang++ in the real command or skip the secondary and record it as 'not compared'.

what: The notebook says clang++'s link errors in this chapter were 'word for word the same (only the final line changes)'. No link step in this chapter was ever run with clang (see the footer finding), and the sentence contradicts itself.
evidence: "Every link message in this chapter came from GNU ld, and clang++ 18 uses the same ld here, so its link errors were word for word the same (only the final line changes, as Chapter 10 showed)." data/cpp-ch28.json: no .cmd program has an `alt` record, and every link step is `g++ main.o ...`.
fix: Replace with: "clang++ 18 hands linking to the same GNU ld here, so its link errors read the same apart from the last line (clang++: error: linker command failed..., as Chapter 10 showed). This chapter's multi-file builds were captured with g++ only."

what: The -DCITY_DEBUG run shows 'The street has 12 lamps' before '[debug] lamps = 12', but a real terminal prints the debug line first.
evidence: debug_flag.cmd has "session": true, so the step that writes to both streams has no `merged` record (known TODO 'From js ch27': session runs record no merged). comic.js outErr() then prints stdout before stderr. A scratch run of the same source with -DCITY_DEBUG, through both `2>&1` and a pty, prints `[debug] lamps = 12` first, then `The street has 12 lamps` (line 6 runs before line 8, and cerr is unbuffered).
fix: Remove "session": true from debug_flag.cmd (its 4 steps don't depend on shell state). The non-session path records `merged`, so recapture and the terminal shows the real order. Alternatively, fix the session merged capture in the engine.

what: The Professor says 'Dennis Ritchie added it [the preprocessor] to C', but the cited source doesn't say who added it.
evidence: Panel 27: "Dennis Ritchie added it to C around 1972 or 1973". Ritchie's 'The Development of the C Language' (fetched from the footer's cs.tufts.edu link) only says: "the most important was the introduction of the preprocessor, partly at the urging of Alan Snyder". It credits later extensions to Mike Lesk and John Reiser. The notebook's history corner words it correctly.
fix: "The preprocessor arrived in C around 1972 or 1973, for file inclusion and simple string replacement, and at first it was an optional extra."

what: The Professor calls an ODR violation 'undefined behaviour, no error required'. The standard's term is 'ill-formed, no diagnostic required'.
evidence: "The standard calls that an ODR violation: undefined behaviour, no error required."
fix: "The standard calls that an ODR violation: the program is broken, but no compiler or linker is required to tell you (\"ill-formed, no diagnostic required\"). In practice, behaviour is unpredictable."

what: The lab says deleting the final bell.notify_one() makes cv_orders freeze, but it only freezes sometimes.
evidence: "In cv_orders.cpp, delete the final bell.notify_one();. The program now freezes at the end". In scratch (line 41 deleted, g++ -std=c++23), 6 runs under `timeout 2` gave exit 0,0,0,0,0,124: one freeze in six. When the waiter is still busy serving, it re-checks `closed` in wait() before sleeping and goes home without a ding.
fix: "...The program may now freeze at the end (run it several times; press Ctrl+C if it hangs). Why does it only sometimes wait forever?" This also teaches the lost-wakeup idea.

what: Claims about other standard libraries are neither captured nor sourced, and one is inaccurate: libc++ also doubles vector capacity.
